title: Top 5 Redis Use Cases

segments.text: In this video, we discovered the versatility of Redis.
We'll talk about the top use cases that have been better tested in production, a
various companies, and a various scales.
Getting insights into how Redis solves interesting skills and ability challenges for us.
And learn why it is a great tool to know well in our system design tool set.
Let's dive right into it.
First of all, what is Redis and why do people use it?
Redis is an in-memory data structure store, it's most commonly used as a cache.
It supports many data structures, such as strings, hashes, lists, sets, and sort of sets.
Redis is known for its speed, we may have video to explain why Redis is so fast.
Look for the link in the description you would like to watch that video.
Now let's dive into the top use cases of Redis.
The number one use case, Redis, is caching objects to speed up web applications.
In this use case, Redis source frequently requests the data in memory.
It allows the web servers to return frequently accessed data quickly.
This reduces the low on the database and improves the response time for the application.
As scale, the cache is distributed among a cluster of Redis servers.
Harding is a common technique to distribute and caching low evenly across the cluster.
Other topics to consider when deploying Redis as a distributed cache include setting a correct
TTL and handling thundering herd on co-start.
Another common use case is to use Redis as a session store to share session data among
stateless servers.
When a user locks into a web application, the session data is stored in Redis, along
with a unique session ID that is returned to the client as a cookie.
When a user makes a request to the application, the session ID is included in the request,
and the stateless web server retrieves the session data from Redis using the ID.
Now it is important to note that Redis is an in-memory database.
The session data stored in Redis will be lost if the Redis servers restarts.
Even though Redis provides persistent options by a snapshot and AOF or a Pan-only file,
they allow session data to be saved to disk and reload in the memory in the event of a restart.
These options often takes too long to low to be practical.
In production, the application is usually used instead.
In this case, data is replicated to a backup instance.
In the event of a crash of the Ming instance, the backup instance is quickly promoted to
take over the traffic.
The next use case is Distributed Lock.
Distributed Locks are used when multiple notes in an application
need to coordinate access to some share resource.
Redis is used as a Distributed Lock, with its atomic commands lie set and next,
or set if not exists.
It allows a caller to set a key, only if it does not already exist.
This is how it works at a high level.
Client 1 tries to acquire the lock by setting a key with a unique value and a time out using the set and X command.
If the key was not already set, the set and X command returns 1, indicating that the lock has been acquired by Client 1.
Client 1 finishes its work and releases the lock by deleting the key.
Now if the key was already set, the set and X command returns 0.
indicating that the lock has already been held by another Client.
In this case, Client 1 waits and retries the set and X operation,
until the lock is released by the other Client.
Note that this simple implementation might be good enough for many use cases,
but it's not completely fault-tolerant.
For production use, there are many redis-client libraries that provide high quality
distributed lock implementation built right up the box.
Next up is Ray Limiter.
Redis can be used as a Ray Limiter by using its increment command on some counters
and setting expiration times on those counters.
A very basic Ray Limiting algorithm works this way.
For each incoming request, the request IP or use ID is used as a key.
The number request for the key is increment to using the increment command in redis.
The current count is compared to the allow rate limit.
If the count is within the Ray Limit, the request is processed.
If the count is over the limit, the request is rejected.
The key is set to expire after a specific time window.
For example, a minute, to reset the counts for the next time window.
Most sophisticated Ray Limiter's, like the leaky bucket algorithm,
can also be implemented using redis.
The last new case we would like to talk about is gaming leaderboard.
For most games, they are not super high-scale.
Redis is a delightful way to implement various types of gaming leaderboards.
Soda sets are the fundamental data structure that enables this.
A Soda set is a collection of unique elements, each with a score associated with it.
The elements are sorted by score.
This allows for quick retrieval of the elements by score in logarithmic time.
That's it for our top Redis use cases.
Whereas it's very versatile.
There are many different ways to use it.
Some features are more better tested than others.
Our creativity is a limit.
Use it with care and have fun with it.
